body:
I can confirm this after having worked in the past with such particular shader. My thoughts so far is that it really is just a massive shader, even though most of it usually gets eliminated (especially if noise settings are hardcoded). 
For me on a Ryzen 5 3.4 GHz it used to freeze for a few seconds (for hardcoded noise params).

Maybe it should be compiled in the background, though that opens the following questions:
- What happens if the shader changes multiple times while it is already compiling in background? Maybe it should not attempt recompiling if already compiling, and when a compilation finishes, if the shader has been modified since, trigger another (i.e only one compilation ongoing at a time, instead of piling up many?)
- How to show to the user (in a non-blocking way) that the shader is actually being compiled under the hood? This becomes important when such compilation takes a while, because otherwise there is no feedback.

Having shaders compiled in the background would probably be the best solution for avoiding freezing the editor in my opinion. As for how, your suggestion sounds good, maybe there could be some icon in shader editor or in the viewport to show when it's being compiled. Another idea could be to have an on-demand button to run the shader compilation, that way the developer can choose when they want to see their changes?

I would also like to ask for any ideas on how I could improve my performance with this for now, I understand that it's a large shader but I don't think my pc should be needing 1-2 minutes for it every time in comparison with my laptop. Is this some Intel vs AMD difference or am I missing something? Is there any way I could look into this more or debug it?

I've noticed that when using a sampler3D uniform and then creating a NoiseTexture3D for that field and changing parameters of the noise, the texture can sometimes also take a while to update/generate. This however is done in the background and does not block the main editor process. (There is also no indication to the user that the noise texture is currently generating in the UI).

So this seems to be generally a problem with FastNoiseLite, although it takes a lot less time when creating the NoiseTexture3D, though that might be because the resolution for that is likely a lot lower than what I have encountered when using it directly in shader code for a sky shader?

Also a side note for using a NoiseTexture3D instead, the quality is generally a lot worse than what I've been doing so far using the GLSL directly. In general the combination of the three dimensions leaves a lot of sharp seams in the image and even using the seamless toggle doesn't help all that much either.

I suggest [using a C++ profiler](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/contributing/development/debugging/using_cpp_profilers.html) on a build with debug symbols enabled to find the exact bottleneck.

Thanks for the pointer! So I built v4.4.1-stable of Godot with debug symbols and used Hotspot to profile the project that I'm having issues with.

Also first I want to mention that I triggered the freeze this time by multiplying the frequency value for the noise in the shader code, even just multiplying the value by 1.0 causes this issue. Another thing to note is that I have the frequency value as a uniform and when I change the value through the inspector the shader in the viewport changes instantly without any freezing whatsoever, so this seems to be mainly linked to editing the shader code.

As for the results I got from Hotspot, I'm not very familiar with the software or with profiling C++ programs so I do apologize for the lack of insight, please do let me know if I can provide any more meaningful information and I'll look into it.

Here's an overview of the Flame Graph:
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/063e47e7-d733-4580-b1de-2e5858a38aae)

Most of the cycles end up with libvulkan_radeon.so, I'm not sure what that entails.

Please let me know what else or what kind of details I should share, I will also be looking more into profiling myself so that I can hopefully be more useful in this case.
